parts: Weather is the state of the atmosphere over a small area at a point of time and changes often; climate is the sum total of weather conditions over a large area for a long period (more than 30 years). India has a monsoon climate.

1. Location (latitude): places nearer the equator are hotter. The Tropic of Cancer divides India into a tropical south and a sub-tropical north. 2. Distance from the sea: coastal areas have an equable climate; interior places like Delhi have an extreme climate. 3. Altitude: temperature falls with height — Shimla is cooler than Ludhiana. 4. Mountain ranges: the Himalayas block cold Central Asian winds and make the monsoon winds shed rain in India; the Western Ghats cause heavy rain on their western slopes. 5. Surface winds: in winter winds blow from land to sea (cold, dry); in summer from sea to land (moist, rain-bearing). 6. Upper-air currents: jet streams blow at about 12,000 m; in winter they bring western disturbances from the Mediterranean that give rain to north-west India, and their northward shift in summer helps the onset of the monsoon.

'Monsoon' comes from the Arabic word 'mausim', meaning season — a seasonal reversal of wind direction. In summer intense heat over north-west India (45–47°C) creates a low-pressure 'monsoon trough' from Jaisalmer to Balasore, while the Indian Ocean is cooler with high pressure. Winds blow from the sea towards the land from the south-west, opposite to the winter north-east trade winds. Being moisture-laden, they give 80–90% of India's annual rain between June and September.

Characteristics: monsoons are irregular and uncertain (early or late); rainfall is unequally distributed (Kerala, West Bengal and Odisha get heavy rain, Haryana and Madhya Pradesh less); the sudden heavy onset is the 'burst of the monsoon', mainly on the Kerala coast; there are 'breaks' — wet and dry spells.

(a) Cold weather season (December–February): temperature decreases from south to north (12–15°C in the north, about 25°C in the south); frost in the north-west; light rain from western disturbances helps rabi crops; snow on the Himalayas. North-east trade winds blow from land to sea, so the season is dry — except the Tamil Nadu coast, where these winds pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and give winter rain.

(b) Hot weather season (March–May): high temperatures in the plains, west and central India; the monsoon trough forms; hot, dry 'loo' winds blow over the northern plains; dust storms in the north-west; violent thunderstorms called 'Kaal Baisakhi' in West Bengal; pre-monsoon 'mango showers' in Kerala and Karnataka help mangoes ripen.

(c) Advancing south-west monsoon season (June–September): winds from the south-west reach the Andaman and Nicobar Islands in late May and the Kerala coast in the first week of June. The Arabian Sea branch, blocked by the Western Ghats, gives heavy rain on their western side and reaches Mumbai by 10 June; the Deccan beyond is a rain-shadow area. The Bay of Bengal branch strikes the north-east and West Bengal and turns west along the plains, with rain decreasing westward (Kolkata 120 cm, Allahabad 91 cm, Delhi 56 cm). The whole country is covered by 15 July. Floods and droughts occur.

(d) Retreating monsoon season (October–November): the monsoon withdraws; hot and humid 'October heat' in the north; the low pressure shifts to the Bay of Bengal, producing tropical cyclones that hit Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, especially the Mahanadi, Godavari and Krishna deltas.

Rainfall is very uneven: it decreases from east to west in the northern plains and from the coast to the interior in the peninsula, and increases with altitude in the north-east. Heavy (over 200 cm): the west coast, sub-Himalayan north-east and the Garo, Khasi and Jaintia hills of Meghalaya. Moderate (100–200 cm): parts of the Western Ghats, West Bengal, Odisha, Bihar. Low (60–100 cm): parts of UP, Rajasthan and the interior Deccan. Inadequate (below 60 cm): western Rajasthan, Gujarat, Ladakh and the south-central part. India has both one of the rainiest and one of the driest places in the world.

Agriculture follows the seasons: kharif crops are sown with the monsoon, rabi crops in winter and zaid crops at the end of winter. Festivals match harvests and seasons — Makar Sankranti, Lohri and Pongal in January, Basant Panchami, Holi and Baisakhi, Onam in Kerala, Dussehra, Durga Puja and Diwali after the monsoon. Urbanisation, industrialisation, deforestation and burning fossil fuels raise CO2 and CFCs; these greenhouse gases trap heat (global warming), disturbing the cycle of seasons and threatening agriculture, on which about 70% of Indians depend.
